497.quote: Content words contain at least two vowels. Some functors, such as the conjunction ma ‘and’, are monosyllabic. This includes double vowels (sequences of two identical vowels) /ii/, /ee/, /aa/, /oo/ and /uu/. Such double vowels are realised phonetically as a single long vowel, i.e. [iː], [ɛː], [aː], [ɔː] and [uː]. Given the placement of stress, one member of a vowel sequence will always bear stress.

tn.translation: Manchu has stress accent (stress). A stressed syllable in Manchu is produced by the speaker with more energy, is longer and has greater intensity. Also, the pitch of a stressed syllable in principle begins with high pitch, but … Stress shift gives rise to a phenomenon resembling tone. For example, [tʲʰamː˩˥(˧)] 'to light' and [tʲʰam˥(˧)] 'to be lit' have the same consonants and vowel but differ in pitch. However, [tʲʰamː˩˥(˧)] also has the pronunciation [tʲʰa˩.ˈvɨm˥(˧)]. Moreover, the examples of this tone-like phenomenon are only a handful and do not form a system. Therefore it is considered that it cannot be called tone.

tn.note: Not a tone language: Manchu has stress accent; a stressed syllable normally begins high (H, or falling when word-final). A few pitch-only pairs arise from stress shift but form no tone system.

qtr.text: Mwotlap has neither tone nor distinctive (contrastive) stress. Word stress falls systematically on its last syllable: e.g. M̄otlap [ŋmʷotˈlap], na-mtevu-ytêl [namtevujˈtɛl]. As in French, this final stress is explained diachronically by the historical loss of post-tonic vowels. If a word is itself part of a phrase, it is the last syllable of the phrase that carries the main stress – following exactly the same rules as French. [n.2] And not on the penultimate, contra Crowley (2002: 588).

dqtr.text: Conversely, two autonomous lexemes will each be provided with their own stress, even if the last word of the phrase bears a stronger stress than the first: cf. tamayge toron̄ # tamayˈge # toˈron̄ # 'a drunk old man'.

evidence_works.detail: The thesis body has no stress section; the appendix reproduces Geytenbeek's pronunciation guide: 'As a primary rule stress should be placed on the first syllable of each word... In words of four or five syllables, the second-to-last syllable is also stressed, though more lightly than the first.' (p. 72). That is initial main stress with secondary on syllable 3 of four-syllable and syllable 4 of five-syllable words, the same as the record's 1010 / 10010; it is silent on six-syllable words. It adds a segmental detail absent from the 2015 sketch: 'A predictable exception occurs only in words of five or more phonemes, and only when sequences within such words begin with /k/, /p/, or /t/, are followed by /i/ or /u/, and then by /r/ or /w/. In such cases the first vowel is shortened or even omitted, and if there would have been stress on that vowel it is transferred onto the next vowel, which is then sometimes slightly lengthened.' (p. 72), with examples pirirri -> "pri:rri", kuwarri -> "kwa:rri", yunturi -> "yuntri". This is a vowel-reduction/syncope process that moves surface stress off a deleted first vowel, not a different placement rule, and it is a secondhand report of Geytenbeek, so it is recorded as detail only.

evidence_works.note: Section '3 Acento' (p. 141) is a literature synthesis with no stress data of its own. It reports the word-final rule of Barros 1987, Aguiar 1985/1988/1994/2003 and the Novas Tribos missionaries (1977a), and records the divergence between descriptions: Barros (1987, p. 67) allows final, penult or antepenult stress in words of more than two syllables, with oscillation attributed to speed and style; Oliveira (1985) says the speech chain can move stress off the last syllable but that all words bear final stress in isolation; Falchi & Aguiar (2011) report words with penult stress. Falchi's own closing summary (via Aguiar 1988, p. 20) is that word-level intensity stress falls systematically on the last syllable and is not distinctive.

512.dq: Stress is non-phonemic since it occurs on the first syllable of words. With the occurrence of the transitional vocoid [ə], phonetically the stress comes on the second syllable, but phonemically it is only one syllable. ... Words of two or more syllables may have secondary stress on the final syllable, and in many of these cases the words can be identified as compound words.
512.prule: Primary stress is non-phonemic and falls on the first syllable of the word; a transitional [ə] that breaks up an initial consonant cluster is not counted as a syllable (phonetically [kəˈlubaʔ] /klubak/, stress on the first phonemic syllable).

sources.text: Stress is the main means of distinguishing word boundaries in Pnar. The final syllable of a word carries heavier stress than preceding syllables, creating minor-major syllable pairings. This provides strong evidence for deciding whether or not clitics and other grammatical morphemes are constituents of a word or function on their own as individual words (see Chapter 3 for a definition of 'word' in Pnar).

514.dq: Prosodic features – a phonological word always retains primary stress on its final syllable, indicating a word boundary.
514.srule: None rhythmic: Ring self-codes WALS 17A 'Absent: no rhythmic stress' (p. 572). Non-final syllables of the phonological word are uniformly lighter than the stressed final syllable; Ring's one use of 'secondary stress' (p. 60, ex. 6 ˈrkʰaj ˌu=ˌmalˈŋiaŋ) marks every pre-final syllable, a minor/major notation rather than an additional stress peak. In compounds of polysyllabic words each member keeps its own final stress (p. 73); Ring & Anderson 2018 (pp. 24-25) likewise read two pitch peaks in 4-syllable words as two phonological words, each with final stress.
